How to Fill Out a Timesheet: Hours, Decimals, and Overtime Worked Out

Direct AnswerFill out a timesheet the right way: convert minutes to decimals, subtract unpaid breaks, total the week, and price overtime — worked out on a $22-an-hour week.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 7, 2026•12 min read•Payroll & Compensation
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: One Formula, Five StepsWhat a Timesheet Is — and What Goes on OneMinutes to Decimals: The Conversion Payroll UsesA Full Week, Worked Out: 42.75 Hours at $22 an HourBreaks: Which Ones Come Off Your TotalThe 7-Minute Rule: What Rounding Costs YouOvernight Shifts and Split ShiftsThe Biweekly Trap: Overtime Is Per Week, Not Per PeriodSix Mistakes That Shrink Your PaycheckHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

A timesheet turns clock-in and clock-out times into paid hours with one formula: (clock-out − clock-in) − unpaid break, converted to decimals. On a $22-an-hour week of 42.75 hours — 40 regular hours plus 2.75 at time and a half — that is $970.75 gross and $821.92 after 2026 federal tax and FICA. The rest of this guide works that week out day by day, then prices the rounding rule, the overnight shift, and the biweekly overtime trap most guides skip.

The Short Answer: One Formula, Five Steps

Filling out a timesheet is five steps, and the same five steps work on paper, in a spreadsheet, or in an app. Here they are, with the headline numbers from the worked week this guide carries through every section — a warehouse associate at $22.00 an hour, Monday to Friday, with a 30-minute lunch most days and a 45-minute lunch on Wednesday:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — One day(Clock-out − clock-in) − unpaid break, in decimals8.00 to 9.25 hours a day
Step 2 — The week8.00 + 8.50 + 9.25 + 8.00 + 9.0042.75 hours
Step 3 — Regular pay40.00 hours × $22.00$880.00
Step 4 — Overtime pay2.75 hours × $33.00 (time and a half)$90.75
Step 5 — Gross for the week$880.00 + $90.75$970.75
Step 6 — Take-home sketchAnnualised $50,479.00; federal $3,877.48; FICA $3,861.64$821.92 a week

The honesty note: the take-home figure annualises this one week — it assumes all 52 weeks look like it, which no real year does. It is there so you can see what the week is worth after tax, not as a promise about your year. The $821.92 is also a cross-check: a flat 40-hour week at the same $22.00 rate is $45,760 a year and $38,948.16 of take-home, which our $22-an-hour guide works out in full — this week’s overtime pattern adds $4,719.00 of gross and $3,791.72 of take-home to that baseline. The five steps below explain every number in the table, starting with what a timesheet actually is.

What a Timesheet Is — and What Goes on One

A timesheet — also called a time card — is the record of the hours you worked over a pay period, and it is the document payroll uses to build your paycheck. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act the employer has to keep accurate time records for every non-exempt employee, but in practice the worker fills the sheet in and the manager signs it off. Whether it is paper, a spreadsheet, or an app, the fields are the same:

FieldWhat goes in itWhy it matters
Name and employee IDYour full name as it appears on your contractPayroll matches names exactly; a nickname can hold up your pay
Pay periodReal start and end dates, e.g. Nov 2–6, 2026A wrong range is one of the most common causes of a delayed check
DateOne row per day worked; leave days off blankBlank rows are skipped; a missing row is not the same as a day off
Clock-in / clock-outThe actual times, in one format all weekMixing 12-hour and 24-hour formats is how AM/PM errors happen
Unpaid breakMinutes, or start and end times, of the meal breakThe only break that comes off your total — see the breaks section
Daily totalWorked hours for that day, in decimalsThis is the number payroll reads, not the clock times
Weekly total and overtimeSum of the days, split at 40 hoursOvertime is priced per workweek, never per pay period
SignatureYours, then your manager’sSign-off is what releases the sheet to payroll

Two habits prevent most timesheet problems before they start. First, fill it in daily, as the shift happens — by Friday afternoon nobody remembers Tuesday’s start time accurately, and a guessed time is how a 7-minute rounding loss or a forgotten lunch becomes a permanent error. Second, pick one time format and stick to it all week: either 12-hour time with AM or PM on every entry, or 24-hour time (08:00, 17:00). The 24-hour format removes the AM/PM flip entirely, which is why most timekeeping systems use it — 5:00 PM is 17:00, and midnight is 00:00. Our pay-stub guide shows where these same hours land on the finished paycheck, and our paychecks-per-year guide explains how the pay period on this sheet decides how many checks you get.

Minutes to Decimals: The Conversion Payroll Uses

Payroll systems do not work in hours and minutes — they work in decimal hours, because decimals add and multiply cleanly. The conversion is one division: decimal hours = hours + (minutes ÷ 60). The minutes that come up every day are worth memorising, because they are the same numbers on every timesheet you will ever fill in:

MinutesDecimalMinutesDecimal
5 minutes0.0830 minutes0.50
6 minutes0.1042 minutes0.70
10 minutes0.1745 minutes0.75
15 minutes0.2550 minutes0.83
20 minutes0.3360 minutes1.00

Worked example, Step/Math/Result style: 7 hours 42 minutes = 7 + (42 ÷ 60) = 7 + 0.70 = 7.70 hours. That 7.70 is the number that goes in the daily-total column — not 7:42, and not 7.42. The classic mistake is writing the minutes straight into the decimal: 8 hours 30 minutes is 8.50, never 8.30, because 8.30 in decimal means 8 hours and 18 minutes (0.30 × 60 = 18). That one slip costs 12 minutes a day — 0.20 hours × $22.00 is $4.40 a day, $22.00 a week, and $1,144.00 over a year of five-day weeks. The same division runs in reverse when you read a card back: 8.25 hours is 8 hours and 15 minutes (0.25 × 60 = 15), and 8.33 is 8 hours and 20 minutes. Our full-time-hours guide uses the same decimal convention for the 30-, 35-, and 40-hour weeks, and the time-card calculator takes daily hours in decimals, so this conversion is the step that connects the paper card to the tool.

A Full Week, Worked Out: 42.75 Hours at $22 an Hour

Here is the anchor week from the short answer, day by day, exactly as it would sit on a paper card. Notice that no two days are identical — real weeks never are — and that the lunch column is what turns elapsed time into paid time:

DayClock-inClock-outUnpaid lunchElapsedWorked (decimal)
Monday8:00 AM4:30 PM30 min8 h 30 m8.00
Tuesday8:05 AM5:05 PM30 min9 h 00 m8.50
Wednesday8:00 AM6:00 PM45 min10 h 00 m9.25
Thursday7:45 AM4:15 PM30 min8 h 30 m8.00
Friday8:00 AM5:30 PM30 min9 h 30 m9.00
Week total45 h 30 m42.75

Each day follows the same three moves. Monday: 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM is 8 hours 30 minutes elapsed; minus the 30-minute lunch, that is 8.00 hours. Wednesday is the long day: 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM is 10 hours elapsed; minus the 45-minute lunch (0.75), that is 9.25 hours. Thursday starts early and ends early — 7:45 AM to 4:15 PM is still 8 hours 30 minutes elapsed, and still 8.00 hours after lunch. Add the five daily totals and the week is 42.75 hours, of which 2.75 sit above the 40-hour federal overtime line:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Weekly hours8.00 + 8.50 + 9.25 + 8.00 + 9.0042.75 hours
Step 2 — Regular hoursFirst 40.00 hours × $22.00$880.00
Step 3 — Overtime hours42.75 − 40.00 = 2.75 hours × $33.00$90.75
Step 4 — Gross for the week$880.00 + $90.75$970.75
Step 5 — Annualised gross$970.75 × 52 weeks$50,479.00
Step 6 — Federal income taxTaxable $34,379.00: $1,240.00 + 12% × $21,979.00$3,877.48
Step 7 — FICA7.65% × $50,479.00$3,861.64
Step 8 — Take-home for the week($50,479.00 − $3,877.48 − $3,861.64) ÷ 52$821.92

Two details in that table are worth pausing on. First, the overtime premium on this week is only $30.25 — the 2.75 overtime hours earn $33.00 instead of $22.00, so the premium is 2.75 × $11.00; the other $60.50 of the $90.75 is straight-time pay those hours would have earned anyway. Second, the take-home works out to $19.23 an hour across the 42.75 hours, against $22.00 gross — the gap is the 2026 federal tax and FICA on a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction, with no state tax and no 401(k) or health premium taken off. Our $22-an-hour guide prices the same rate with no overtime at all, and our double-time guide shows what happens when the multiplier is 2× instead of 1.5×.

Breaks: Which Ones Come Off Your Total

The most common timesheet error is deducting the wrong breaks. Federal law draws one clean line, and it is the length of the break that decides which side of it you are on:

BreakLengthCounts as hours worked?What to write
Rest break (coffee, stretch, bathroom)5 to 20 minutesYes — paidDo not deduct it; it stays inside your daily total
Meal break (lunch, dinner)30 minutes or moreNo — unpaidDeduct it, as in the worked week above
On-duty meal30 minutes, still workingYes — paidDo not deduct it; note that you stayed on duty

The rule comes from the Fair Labor Standards Act regulations: rest breaks of 5 to 20 minutes are compensable work time (29 CFR 785.18), and a meal period of 30 minutes or more is not, as long as you are fully relieved of duty — free to leave the work area and do what you like (29 CFR 785.19). Worked example on the anchor week’s Monday: 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM with two 15-minute paid rest breaks and a 30-minute unpaid lunch is 8.00 paid hours, not 7.50 — the two 15-minute breaks stay inside the total, and only the lunch comes off. The grey area is the 21-to-29-minute break: the regulations do not name it, so employers usually treat anything under 30 minutes as paid rest time, but the safe move is to ask payroll how yours is coded rather than guessing. State law can add a second layer on top of the federal rule — California requires a 30-minute meal period after 5 hours of work, and several other states set their own meal and rest rules — so the federal table above is the floor, not the whole law in your state. Our daily-overtime guide shows how the same kind of state-by-state variation works for overtime, and our paycheck-tax guide explains why the gross figure and the take-home figure on your stub are two different numbers.

The 7-Minute Rule: What Rounding Costs You

Most employers do not pay to the minute. They round punches to the nearest 5, 6, or 15 minutes, and the most common version is quarter-hour rounding under 29 CFR 785.48 — the rule everyone calls the 7-minute rule:

Your actual punchRounded toMinutes gained or lost
Clock in 8:01 to 8:078:00You lose 1 to 7 minutes
Clock in 8:08 to 8:148:15You gain 1 to 7 minutes
Clock out 4:53 to 4:594:45You lose 1 to 7 minutes
Clock out 5:00 to 5:075:00You lose 0 to 7 minutes

The rule is legal only if it averages out fairly over time — the regulation’s own test is that rounding must not consistently favour the employer. That is the part most guides leave out, and it is the part with money in it. Take a worker who always arrives at 8:07 and always leaves at 5:07. Every day the clock-in rounds down to 8:00 (7 minutes lost) and the clock-out rounds down to 5:00 (7 minutes lost): 14 minutes a day, 70 minutes a week, 1.17 hours a week. At $22.00 an hour that is $25.67 a week, or $1,334.67 over a year of five-day weeks — and the rounding never once rounds in the worker’s favour, so it fails the fairness test the regulation sets. The honest note in the other direction: the same rule can pay you for minutes you did not work — clocking in at 8:08 is recorded as 8:15, seven free minutes — which is exactly why the rule survives: it is supposed to cut both ways. What to do about it: keep your own log of actual in and out times for two weeks, compare it with the rounded card, and if the rounding always cuts against you, raise it with payroll with the log in hand. A one-sided pattern is a fact you can show; a feeling about the clock is not.

Overnight Shifts and Split Shifts

Two shift shapes break the simple formula, and both are common enough to need their own worked example. The first is the overnight shift, where the clock-out time is earlier than the clock-in time. The fix is to add 12 hours to the out time before subtracting — or, simpler, to count forward across midnight: 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM is 2 hours to midnight plus 6 hours after it, which is 8 hours elapsed. Minus a 30-minute meal break, that is 7.50 hours, or $165.00 at $22.00 an hour. The trap is the workweek boundary: if your workweek runs Sunday to Saturday and the shift starts Saturday night and ends Sunday morning, the hours land in different weeks depending on your employer’s policy, and that decides which week the overtime falls in — ask payroll which day they use, because a 7.50-hour shift can be the difference between 39.50 hours (no overtime) and 47.00 hours (7.00 at time and a half) in the week it lands in. The second shape is the split shift: two blocks in one day with a long unpaid gap between them, for example 7:00 AM to 11:00 AM and 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM. That is 4.00 + 4.00 = 8.00 hours, and the six-hour gap in the middle is unpaid time, not a break to deduct — you were not on the clock at all. Some states add a split-shift premium on top of the hours; federal law does not, so check your own state’s rule before assuming the 8.00 hours is the whole story.

The Biweekly Trap: Overtime Is Per Week, Not Per Period

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, overtime is calculated on a fixed seven-day workweek — never on the pay period as a whole. That distinction is invisible on weekly pay and worth $55.00 on biweekly pay. Take two weeks at $22.00 an hour: week one is 45 hours, week two is 35 hours. The period total is 80 hours, and the wrong way to price it is 80 × $22.00 = $1,760.00. The right way is week by week: week one is 40 × $22.00 + 5 × $33.00 = $1,045.00, week two is 35 × $22.00 = $770.00, and the period total is $1,815.00 — $55.00 more than the period-total method. The same rule applies on every schedule, with one complication each:

ScheduleHow overtime is countedWhat to watchLimitation
WeeklyHours over 40 in the one workweekNothing hidden — the period is the workweekDaily overtime in five states is separate; see our daily-overtime guide
BiweeklyEach of the two workweeks separatelyA 45-hour week next to a 35-hour week still pays 5 overtime hoursThe period total of 80 hours tempts payroll software and workers alike to skip the split
SemimonthlyStill per seven-day workweekPeriods run 13 to 16 days and cut workweeks in halfThe split has to be done by payroll; check the stub, because the sheet itself hides it

Semimonthly pay is where the trap is hardest to spot, because a 15-day period never lines up with a 7-day workweek — the period boundary falls in the middle of a workweek, and the overtime for that split week has to be reconstructed from the daily rows. That is one reason employers who pay hourly workers usually choose biweekly instead. If your stub shows a biweekly period total of 80.00 hours and $1,760.00 of gross at $22.00 an hour with no overtime line, while your card shows a 45-hour week in it, the $55.00 is missing — and the fix is the two weekly rows, not an argument about the period total. Our biweekly-versus-semimonthly comparison runs the two schedules through a full year on the same $60,000 salary, and our overtime-rules-by-state page lists the five states where daily overtime adds a second threshold on top of the weekly one.

Six Mistakes That Shrink Your Paycheck

Every mistake below is one this guide has already priced, so the cost is not abstract. Run through them against your own card before you submit it:

  1. Writing 8.30 for 8 hours 30 minutes. 8.30 in decimal is 8 hours and 18 minutes — 12 minutes short a day, $22.00 a week, $1,144.00 a year at $22.00 an hour. Write 8.50.
  2. Flipping AM and PM. 5:00 without the PM is 5:00 AM, and a 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM shift becomes a negative number or a 20-hour day. Use 24-hour time (17:00) and the error disappears.
  3. Forgetting the unpaid lunch. Leaving the 30 minutes in adds 0.50 hours a day you did not work — $11.00 a day, $55.00 a week — and payroll will catch it and claw it back, usually on the next check.
  4. Leaving a missing punch blank. A day with no out time usually pays $0 until someone corrects it. Report it the same day with the real time you left.
  5. Counting overtime on the period total. 45 hours plus 35 hours is not 80 straight hours — it is $1,815.00, not $1,760.00. Overtime is per workweek, always.
  6. Letting rounding cut one way. Seven minutes lost at both ends of every shift is $25.67 a week and $1,334.67 a year at $22.00 an hour. Keep your own log for two weeks and compare.

The five-minute check before you submit: (1) every day has an in, an out, and a lunch; (2) every daily total is in decimals, not hours:minutes; (3) the lunch is subtracted once, not twice and not zero times; (4) the weekly total is the sum of the daily totals, and the overtime line is the part above 40; (5) the period dates on the sheet match the dates payroll expects. If all five pass, the sheet is ready for the manager’s signature.

How to Use the Calculator

Run the anchor week through the time-card calculator in four steps — and watch for the one place where the tool needs a hand adjustment:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your hourly rate: $22.00. This is the rate the regular and overtime lines are priced at.
  2. Step 2 — Enter each day’s hours before unpaid breaks: the elapsed hours from the table — Monday 8.50, Tuesday 9.00, Wednesday 10.00, Thursday 8.50, Friday 9.50. Use 0 for days off; the calculator skips them.
  3. Step 3 — Enter the unpaid break minutes and the overtime settings: 30 minutes per worked day, threshold 40 hours a week, multiplier 1.5. The calculator deducts the break from each day, then splits the week at 40 hours.
  4. Step 4 — Adjust Wednesday by hand: the calculator takes one break value for the whole week, and Wednesday’s lunch was 45 minutes, not 30. Its result is $979.00 on 43.00 hours; subtract the extra 15 minutes at the overtime rate — 0.25 × $33.00 = $8.25 — and you land exactly on the hand-worked $970.75. That match is the proof the week is right.

Limitations

  1. Federal only unless stated: the take-home sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction. State and local taxes are excluded, so actual take-home is lower in most states.
  2. One week annualised: the $821.92 take-home assumes all 52 weeks look like the anchor week. Real weeks vary, and a week with no overtime annualises to $38,948.16 instead — the $22-an-hour guide’s figure.
  3. Rounding varies by employer: the 7-minute rule is the most common quarter-hour system, but some employers round to 5 or 6 minutes, and some do not round at all. Your employer’s written policy is the rule that applies to you.
  4. State law adds layers: meal and rest-break rules, split-shift premiums, and daily overtime thresholds differ by state. This guide states the federal position and one California example; check your own state’s labor department for the rule that applies to you.
  5. The calculator takes one break value: the time-card calculator applies a single unpaid-break figure to every worked day. Weeks with different lunches need the hand adjustment shown in the How to Use section.
  6. Overnight attribution is a policy choice: hours that cross midnight land in the workweek your employer’s policy assigns them to. The guide’s example assumes the shift counts in the week it starts; confirm with payroll.
  7. Not tax or legal advice: these are 2026 federal estimates for a single filer taking the standard deduction, using the same method as the site’s other guides. Your employer’s payroll calendar, rounding policy, and benefit deductions change the figures.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about filling out a timesheet, and what each one is worth:

How do you calculate hours worked on a timesheet?

For each day, subtract the clock-in time from the clock-out time, then subtract any unpaid break: (clock-out − clock-in) − unpaid break. Convert the result to decimal hours by dividing the minutes by 60, then add the daily totals for the week. Example: 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM is 8 hours 30 minutes elapsed; minus a 30-minute unpaid lunch, that is 8.00 hours. A five-day week of 8.00, 8.50, 9.25, 8.00, and 9.00 hours totals 42.75 hours — 40 regular hours plus 2.75 at time and a half.

How do you convert minutes to decimal hours?

Divide the minutes by 60 and add the result to the whole hours: decimal hours = hours + (minutes ÷ 60). So 15 minutes is 0.25, 30 minutes is 0.50, 45 minutes is 0.75, and 7 hours 42 minutes is 7.70. The trap is writing the minutes straight into the decimal: 8 hours 30 minutes is 8.50, never 8.30 — 8.30 in decimal means 8 hours and 18 minutes, which is 12 minutes short of what you worked.

What is the 7-minute rule on a time clock?

It is the common name for quarter-hour rounding under 29 CFR 785.48: punches 1 to 7 minutes past a quarter-hour mark round down, and 8 to 14 minutes past round up. Clocking in at 8:07 is recorded as 8:00; clocking in at 8:08 is recorded as 8:15. The rule is only legal if it averages out fairly over time — if it always cuts the same way, it is not neutral. A worker who loses 7 minutes at the start and 7 at the end of every shift loses 70 minutes a week, which is $25.67 a week or $1,334.67 a year at $22 an hour.

Do lunch breaks count as hours worked?

A meal break of 30 minutes or more does not count, as long as you are fully relieved of duty — you can leave the work area and do what you like. Short rest breaks of 5 to 20 minutes do count: federal law treats them as paid work time, and your employer cannot deduct them. So an 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM shift with two 15-minute paid breaks and a 30-minute unpaid lunch is 8.00 paid hours, not 7.50. Some states add their own meal-break rules — California, for example, requires a 30-minute meal period after 5 hours of work.

How many hours is 8:00 to 4:30 with a 30-minute lunch?

8.00 hours. The elapsed time from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM is 8 hours 30 minutes; subtract the 30-minute unpaid lunch and 8 hours remain, written as 8.00 in decimal. The same shift with a 45-minute lunch is 7.75 hours, and with no lunch at all it is 8.50 hours. If your card shows 8.30 for this shift, it is wrong — 8.30 in decimal is 8 hours and 18 minutes.

What happens if you forget to clock out?

The day shows a missing punch, and most payroll systems pay $0 for it until it is corrected — so report it the same day and ask your manager to enter the real out time. Never guess or fill in a round number; write down the time you actually left, and keep your own note of it. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act your employer has to pay for all hours actually worked, even if the punch is missing, but the correction only happens if someone flags it before payroll runs.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • One formula runs the whole sheet: (clock-out − clock-in) − unpaid break, in decimals — on a $22-an-hour week of 42.75 hours that is $970.75 gross and $821.92 after 2026 federal tax and FICA.
  • 8 hours 30 minutes is 8.50, never 8.30 — writing 8.30 costs 12 minutes a day, $22.00 a week, and $1,144.00 a year at $22.00 an hour.
  • Short breaks stay in, long breaks come off — rest breaks of 5 to 20 minutes are paid work time, meal breaks of 30 minutes or more are unpaid if you are fully relieved of duty.
  • Rounding has to cut both ways — seven minutes lost at both ends of every shift is $25.67 a week and $1,334.67 a year at $22.00 an hour, so keep your own log for two weeks and compare.
  • Overtime is per workweek, never per pay period — a 45-hour week next to a 35-hour week pays $1,815.00 at $22.00 an hour, not $1,760.00, and the $55.00 difference is the most common biweekly error.
  • Overnight shifts cross midnight, not the formula — 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM with a 30-minute meal is 7.50 hours and $165.00 at $22.00 an hour, and the workweek boundary decides which week the overtime lands in.
  • Fill the sheet in daily, and run the five-minute check before you submit — every day needs an in, an out, and a lunch; every total needs to be in decimals; the lunch is subtracted once; the overtime line is the part above 40.
  • Check the tool against the hand math — the time-card calculator gives $979.00 on the anchor week before Wednesday’s extra 15 minutes; subtract 0.25 × $33.00 and you land exactly on $970.75.

  1. One formula runs the whole sheet: (clock-out − clock-in) − unpaid break, in decimals — on a $22-an-hour week of 42.75 hours that is $970.75 gross and $821.92 after 2026 federal tax and FICA.
